newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - "Euro-bit tax" sparks Internet controversy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Euro-bit tax" sparks Internet controversy.

text.p: A wave of protest from Internet users has greeted the suggestion that the European Union may consider taxing the amount of information users get out of the system.

Luc Soete, who heads an EU advisory group that came up with the idea of taxing every "bit" or electronic unit transmitted, said he has received 300 or 400 electronic mail messages on the subject, most of them negative and at least one abusive.
One called him a "schmuck", others said more mildly: "Hands Off the Internet".
The proposal has also spawned a new World Wide Web site called "Oppose the Euro Bit Tax", which it calls "an insidious and unjustifiable idea."
The controversy reflects the sensitivity of any move to rein in the free-wheeling nature of the Internet and other online networks.
But Soete, director of the Maastricht Economic Research Institute on Innovation and Technology in the Netherlands, said he was surprised by the vehemence of the reaction.
"What I'm taken aback by are the extremely negative comments on the suggestion that research should be done," he told Reuters. "This to me is not scientific."
TAX IMPLICATIONS OF GLOBAL ELECTRONIC COMMERCE
Soete, who says governments must rethink their taxation policies in a new era of global communications, envisages a tax based on the number of bits transmitted.
The idea was first included in an interim report the EU advisory group -- which was asked to study the social implications of the new "information society" -- submitted in January 1996.
Soete later expanded the idea in a paper that was made available on a European Commission Web site.

The advisory group, composed of academics, industry and labour representatives and others, is expected to issue a final report shortly that will mention the "bit tax" in a broader discussion of the tax implications of global electronic commerce, Soete said.
Soete argues that governments need to consider revamping their tax systems to reflect an economy that is increasingly based on "intangible" transactions rather than "tangible", or physical, goods.

Companies offering electronic services such as banking or insurance from abroad can avoid value-added taxes, while traditional providers become less competitive because they cannot escape the taxes, Soete's paper says.
Soete argues that a "bit tax" offers governments a way to recoup lost revenues at a time when they are searching for ways to fund their struggling social security systems.
He recognises that certain aspects of the idea need more study -- for example, whether the impact on demand in Europe would be too severe.
But he sees it as a possible alternative to the high employment taxes in some countries that are accused of hindering Europe's ability to create jobs.
BIT TAX WOULD DRIVE FIRMS OUT OF EUROPE, CRITICS SAY
Those arguments do not wash with Soete's critics, who say a "bit tax" smacks of Big Brother, would be technically impractical and would drive companies out of Europe.

"Given that there is no precedence for such a tax based on other information flows, the Bit Tax would indeed be nothing more than a taxation on the fundamental freedom of speech via the Internet," says the anti-bit tax Web site.
The site was launched by Keith Blakemore-Noble, a British software development manager.
Another EU advisory group, composed of media and telecommunications companies, has drafted a report urging the EU to reject the bit tax.
"New services should not be burdened with new tax schemes, which would inhibit the growth and development of such services, including by diverting them to non-EU jurisdictions," says the draft text.

That group reports to EU Commissioner Martin Bangemann, who is in charge of telecoms and information technologies and opposes the tax, arguing that it would widen the existing competitiveness gap between Europe and the United States.
"Europe's problem is still that communications costs are higher than in other parts of the world," said Jochen Kubosch, Bangemann's spokesman.
But EU Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn, who appointed Soete's group, does not want to prejudge the proposal, said Barbara Nolan, his spokeswoman.

While stressing that the bit tax was not a Commission proposal, Nolan said Flynn was pleased at how seriously the group was taking its job. "We will want to look at whatever they say in their final report," she said.
